title: Aglauros. Invidia
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Mercury, crossing the sky over Athens, looks down on a procession of girls carrying offerings up to Minerva's citadel, and catches fire at the sight of one of them, Herse. He lands — after seeing to his hair and his cloak — and asks her sister Aglauros for the way in; Aglauros names a price in gold. Minerva, who has not forgotten what this girl once uncovered, goes down to the house of Envy. Ovid stops the story to build Envy a body and a home, then sends her to Athens, where what she plants in Aglauros hardens into stone in a doorway.

advisory.lede: A god decides he wants Herse, bargains with her sister for the way into her bedroom, and forces the doors when he is blocked; Herse herself is never asked.
advisory.more: The pursuit takes the opening forty lines and comes back for eight near the end. Ovid gives Mercury a predator's simile — a kite circling entrails it cannot yet reach — and then five comic lines of the god smoothing his hair and setting his cloak before he lands; the comedy and the coercion are the same passage, and the joke is on Mercury's vanity, not at Herse's expense. Herse never speaks. The negotiation happens over her, between a god who names his future children before asking anything and a sister who names a price. What follows the opening of the doors is not narrated: the poem's attention turns to Aglauros, who is destroyed for having stood in the way. Lectorium presents the text unaltered.

sentences.t:
Hinc se sustulerat paribus caducifer alis,
Munychiosque volans agros gratamque Minervae
despectabat humum cultique arbusta Lycei.
sentences.l: From here the caduceus-bearer had lifted himself on level wings, and, flying, was looking down on the Munychian fields and the ground dear to Minerva and the plantations of the well-tended Lyceum.
sentences.i: From there the wand-bearer had risen on level wings, and as he flew he looked down over the fields of Munychia, the ground Minerva loves, and the tree-lined walks of the Lyceum.
sentences.n: Mercury is still airborne out of the tale before this one. 'caducifer', the caduceus-bearer, names him from the herald's staff rather than by name, which is Ovid's habit with this god. The Munychian fields are Attic (Munychia is one of Athens' harbours), the ground 'dear to Minerva' is Attica itself, and the Lyceum is the planted ground outside the walls where Athenians walked; 'despectabat' is imperfect, so he keeps looking for a while.

sentences.t:
Illa forte die castae de more puellae
vertice supposito festas in Palladis arces
pura coronatis portabant sacra canistris.
sentences.l: On that day, as it fell out, chaste girls by custom, with the head put under [the load], were carrying pure holy things in garlanded baskets up into Pallas' festal citadel.
sentences.i: It happened to be the day when, as custom asked, unmarried girls carried the pure offerings in garlanded baskets up to Pallas' citadel for her festival, each balancing her basket on her head.
sentences.n: 'vertice supposito' is an ablative absolute — a self-contained 'with X done' phrase where English wants a clause; here the head is put under the basket, which is how the load is carried. You will meet ablative absolutes constantly in this poem. 'castae puellae' are the unmarried girls of the city, and the wreathed baskets mark a procession up to Athena's citadel: a picture arranged, as it happens, for a god in the air to look down at.

sentences.t:
Inde revertentes deus adspicit ales iterque
non agit in rectum, sed in orbem curvat eundem.
sentences.l: The winged god sees them returning from there, and does not drive his way straight on, but curves it into one and the same circle.
sentences.i: The winged god catches sight of them on their way back, and does not hold his course straight ahead but bends it round into the same circle, again and again.
sentences.n: 'adspicit' is a historic present dropped into a run of past tenses ('sustulerat', 'despectabat', 'portabant'); Latin narrative does this to bring a moment close, and English usually takes it as a plain past. 'eundem' is masculine accusative and agrees with 'orbem' — 'iter' is neuter and cannot take it: the circle is the same one, traced over and over, and the point returns two lines later as 'easdem … auras', the same patch of air. The turn is the first sign that he has seen something he wants.

sentences.t:
Ut volucris visis rapidissima miluus extis,
dum timet et densi circumstant sacra ministri,
flectitur in gyrum nec longius audet abire
spemque suam motis avidus circumvolat alis,
sentences.l: As the kite, swiftest of birds, when the entrails have been sighted, while it is afraid and the attendants stand thick about the offering, wheels into a ring and does not dare go further off, and greedily circles its own hope on beating wings,
sentences.i: As a kite, the quickest thing on wings, once it has spotted the entrails — afraid, with the attendants standing thick around the sacrifice — wheels in a ring and dares go no further off, but circles its hope, greedy, on beating wings,
sentences.n: 'visis extis' is another ablative absolute. The kite is the scavenger that waits at a sacrifice for the god's portion, kept off by the crowd of attendants; 'spem suam', 'its own hope', is a fine swerve, since what the bird circles is not the meat but its wanting of it. Ovid could have given Mercury an eagle. He gives him a thief-bird.

sentences.t:
sic super Actaeas agilis Cyllenius arces
inclinat cursus et easdem circinat auras.
sentences.l: so over the Actaean citadel the nimble Cyllenian leans his course round, and compasses the same air.
sentences.i: so over the citadel of Attica the quick Cyllenian tilts his flight and circles round and round the same patch of sky.
sentences.n: 'Cyllenius' names Mercury from Mount Cyllene in Arcadia, where he was born, and 'Actaeas' is the poetic word for Attic. 'circinat' comes from 'circinus', the compass a draughtsman draws with: he is not merely circling but scribing a neat ring in the air — the same figure the kite drew, done with an instrument.

sentences.t:
Quanto splendidior quam cetera sidera fulget
Lucifer, et quanto quam Lucifer aurea Phoebe,
tanto virginibus praestantior omnibus Herse
ibat, eratque decus pompae comitumque suarum.
sentences.l: By as much as Lucifer shines more brilliantly than the other stars, and by as much as golden Phoebe than Lucifer, by so much did Herse walk more outstanding than all the maidens, and she was the ornament of the procession and of her companions.
sentences.i: By as much as the Morning Star outshines the other stars, and golden Phoebe the Morning Star, by so much did Herse outshine every girl there as she walked; she was the glory of the procession and of the companions in it.
sentences.n: 'quanto … tanto' are ablatives of measure of difference — 'by how much … by so much' — and Ovid runs the ladder up two rungs before putting Herse on the third. Lucifer is the Morning Star, Phoebe the moon. The praise is exact and a little cool: she is a light among lights, seen from the air, by the god who is deciding.

sentences.t:
Obstipuit forma Iove natus, et aethere pendens
non secus exarsit, quam cum Balearica plumbum
funda iacit:
sentences.l: Jove's son was stunned at her beauty, and, hanging in the upper air, blazed up no otherwise than when a Balearic sling hurls its lead:
sentences.i: Jove's son was stunned by her beauty, and hanging there in the high air he caught fire exactly as lead does when a Balearic sling lets it go:
sentences.n: 'forma' is an ablative of cause: stunned by the beauty, not merely at it. Ovid does not say the god fell in love — he says he took fire, and then spends three lines on the ballistics of a sling-bullet. The Balearic islanders were the ancient world's famous slingers, hired as specialists.

sentences.t:
volat illud et incandescit eundo
et quos non habuit, sub nubibus invenit ignes.
sentences.l: it flies, and grows white-hot by the going, and the fires it did not have it finds beneath the clouds.
sentences.i: it flies, and glows white-hot with the going, and finds under the clouds the fire it did not set out with.
sentences.n: 'eundo' is the ablative gerund of 'eo' — 'by going', by the mere fact of travel; the physics is ancient and wrong and lovely, friction with the air kindling the lead in flight. The relative clause is pulled in front of its own noun ('quos … ignes'), which English cannot manage. The joke is that the god, like the bullet, is heating up on the way down.

sentences.t:
Vertit iter caeloque petit terrena relicto
nec se dissimulat: tanta est fiducia formae.
sentences.l: He turns his course and, heaven left behind, makes for the things of earth, and does not disguise himself: so great is his confidence in his beauty.
sentences.i: He turns his course, leaves the sky behind and makes for the ground, and does not trouble to disguise himself: such is his faith in his own looks.
sentences.n: 'caelo relicto' is one more ablative absolute. 'nec se dissimulat' is pointed — gods in this poem almost always arrive in some other shape, and this one comes as himself. The half-line that follows says why: 'tanta est fiducia formae', so great is the confidence he has in his own beauty. The vanity is the joke, and the next five lines prove it.

sentences.t:
Quae quamquam iusta est, cura tamen adiuvat illam
permulcetque comas chlamydemque, ut pendeat apte,
collocat, ut limbus totumque appareat aurum,
sentences.l: And though that confidence is justified, still care helps it along: he smooths his hair and sets his cloak, so that it may hang just so, so that the border and all its gold may show,
sentences.i: And justified though it is, he gives it some help all the same: he smooths his hair, arranges his cloak so that it falls just right and the gold-worked border shows to the last thread,
sentences.n: 'Quae' opening the sentence is a connecting relative — 'and this', picking up 'fiducia' from the line before, not asking a question. Watch for this: 'quae', 'quam', 'quibus' at the head of a sentence usually mean 'and she', 'and it', 'and by these'. The subject of all these verbs is never named; Ovid simply lets the god preen. 'cura' is the word for grooming and for anxiety at once.

sentences.t:
ut teres in dextra, qua somnos ducit et arcet,
virga sit, ut tersis niteant talaria plantis.
sentences.l: so that the polished wand may be in his right hand — the wand with which he draws sleep on and keeps it off — so that his winged sandals may gleam on soles wiped clean.
sentences.i: so that the polished wand sits in his right hand — the wand that brings sleep on and drives it off — and his winged sandals gleam above feet he has wiped clean.
sentences.n: The wand is the caduceus, and 'somnos ducit et arcet' states its two powers in one breath: it gives sleep and takes it away, which is why this is the god sent on errands. 'qua' sits next to 'dextra' but reaches forward to 'virga': it is the wand, not the hand, that does the sleeping and the waking. 'talaria' are the winged sandals at the ankle, and 'tersis plantis' are soles wiped clean. The comedy is in the checklist — a god going over his own equipment like a man at a mirror.

sentences.t:
Pars secreta domus ebore et testudine cultos
tres habuit thalamos:
sentences.l: A withdrawn part of the house held three bedchambers, fitted out with ivory and tortoiseshell:
sentences.i: A private wing of the house held three bedchambers, finished in ivory and tortoiseshell:
sentences.n: 'thalami' are the inner rooms of the women of the household. Ivory and tortoiseshell veneer are the luxury materials of Ovid's own Rome, not of legendary Athens; furnishing the myth with contemporary fittings makes the palace suddenly local, and the three doors suddenly real.

sentences.t:
quorum tu, Pandrose, dextrum,
Aglauros laevum, medium possederat Herse.
sentences.l: of which you, Pandrosos, [held] the right-hand one, Aglauros the left, and Herse had held the middle.
sentences.i: of these you, Pandrosos, had the room on the right, Aglauros the one on the left, and Herse the room between.
sentences.n: Ovid turns aside to address Pandrosos directly. This is apostrophe, one of his standing habits, and the second person should be kept: flattening it to 'Pandrosos had' loses the sudden intimacy of a poet speaking to someone inside his own story. One verb, 'possederat', has to serve all three sisters, so English supplies '[held]' for the first two. The middle room is Herse's, which will matter.

sentences.t:
Quae tenuit laevum, venientem prima notavit
Mercurium nomenque dei scitarier ausa est
et causam adventus.
sentences.l: She who held the left-hand one was the first to mark Mercury coming, and dared to ask the god's name and the reason for his arrival.
sentences.i: The one whose room was on the left was first to notice Mercury coming, and made bold to ask the god his name and what had brought him.
sentences.n: Aglauros is identified sidelong, by her door, one line after she was named. 'scitarier' is an old passive-looking form of the infinitive of the deponent 'scitari', 'to ask' — an archaism that gives the line a formal, epic colour the plain 'scitari' would not. She dares: the boldness is stated before we learn what it will cost.

sentences.t:
Cui sic respondit Atlantis
Pleionesque nepos:
sentences.l: To her the grandson of Atlas and Pleione answered thus:
sentences.i: The grandson of Atlas and Pleione answered her:
sentences.n: 'Cui' is a connecting relative again — 'and to her'. Mercury's mother was Maia, one of the Pleiades, daughters of Atlas and Pleione; the roundabout title is a small piece of showing-off placed just before the god introduces himself by his father instead.

sentences.t:
“Ego sum, qui iussa per auras
verba patris porto: pater est mihi Iuppiter ipse.
sentences.l: “I am the one who carries my father's ordered words through the air: the father I have is Jupiter himself.”
sentences.i: “I am the one who carries my father's orders through the air: my father is Jupiter himself.”
sentences.n: 'pater est mihi Iuppiter ipse' is a dative of possession: Latin says 'the father is to me' where English says 'I have a father'. You will meet this constantly. The self-introduction is all credentials — he is the messenger before he is anyone, and he leads with whose son he is.

sentences.t:
Nec fingam causas; tu tantum fida sorori
esse velis prolisque meae matertera dici.
sentences.l: “And I shall not invent reasons; only be willing to be loyal to your sister, and to be called the mother's-sister of my offspring.”
sentences.i: “And I will not invent excuses; only be willing to stand by your sister — and to be called aunt to my children.”
sentences.n: 'matertera' is precisely the mother's sister, not the father's, and the word only works if Herse is already the mother: the child is in his mouth before the girl has been asked anything at all. 'velis' is a polite subjunctive, 'be so good as to'. The candour and the presumption arrive in the same breath.

sentences.t: Herse causa viae. Faveas oramus amanti.”
sentences.l: “Herse is the cause of the journey. We beg that you favour a lover.”
sentences.i: “Herse is my reason for coming. Show a lover some kindness, I ask you.”
sentences.n: 'Herse causa viae' has no verb at all — four words and no 'is', which is how Latin states a thing flatly; 'via' here is the journey, not the road under his feet. 'oramus' is a first-person plural for a single speaker, the plural of self-importance. 'amanti' is a participle used as a noun, 'one who loves', so that the favour is asked not for him but for a category. Three sentences, and the errand is done.

sentences.t:
Adspicit hunc oculis isdem, quibus abdita nuper
viderat Aglauros flavae secreta Minervae,
sentences.l: Aglauros looks at him with the same eyes with which she had lately seen the hidden secrets of golden-haired Minerva,
sentences.i: Aglauros looks at him with the very eyes that had lately seen what golden-haired Minerva kept hidden,
sentences.n: The sentence opens with its verb and holds the subject's name back to the second line — read 'Adspicit hunc … Aglauros'. 'isdem' is Magnus's spelling of 'eisdem', kept as the edition prints it. What those eyes saw is told four lines further on; for now it is enough that this is a girl who has already looked at what she was told not to look at, and that the goddess has not forgotten it.

sentences.t:
proque ministerio magni sibi ponderis aurum
postulat:
sentences.l: and in return for the service she demands for herself gold of great weight:
sentences.i: and for her services she demands gold, and a great weight of it:
sentences.n: 'magni ponderis' is a genitive of description hung on 'aurum' — gold 'of great weight'. The demand is put in the language of a contract: 'pro ministerio' is payment for a service rendered. She does not refuse the god. She prices him.

sentences.t: interea tectis excedere cogit.
sentences.l: meanwhile she forces him to go out from the house.
sentences.i: and in the meantime she makes him leave the house.
sentences.n: 'tectis' is an ablative of separation with 'excedere', 'out from under the roof' — 'tecta', roofs, is the ordinary poetic word for a house. 'cogit', 'forces', used of a mortal girl and a god standing on her doorstep, is deliberately outrageous: she is bargaining from a position she does not hold.

sentences.t:
Vertit ad hanc torvi dea bellica luminis orbem
et tanto penitus traxit suspiria motu,
sentences.l: The war goddess turned upon her the orb of her grim eye, and drew sighs from deep within with so great a heaving,
sentences.i: The goddess of war turned the circle of her grim eye on her and drew such deep sighs, with such a heave,
sentences.n: 'orbem luminis' makes the eyeball a sphere: Latin can turn a look into a physical object and swing it round like a turret. 'torvi' is the adjective for a bull's stare. The sentence is a long result clause waiting for its 'ut' — the anger will be measured not by her face but by what the sighing does to her armour.

sentences.t:
ut pariter pectus positamque in pectore forti
aegida concuteret.
sentences.l: that it shook alike her breast and the aegis laid on that strong breast.
sentences.i: that her breast and the aegis lying on that strong breast shook together.
sentences.n: The result clause pays off. The aegis is Minerva's goat-skin breastplate with the Gorgon's head set in it; 'pectus … in pectore' repeats the word so that flesh and armour rise together, and we are told how angry a goddess is by watching a shield move.

sentences.t:
Subit, hanc arcana profana
detexisse manu tum cum sine matre creatam
Lemnicolae stirpem contra data foedera vidit,
sentences.l: It comes over her: that this girl uncovered the secret with unhallowed hand, that time when, against the compact given, she looked at the Lemnian-dweller's offspring, made without a mother,
sentences.i: It comes back to her — that this was the girl who lifted the lid with unhallowed hand and looked, against the promise she had given, at the motherless child of the Lemnian god.
sentences.n: 'Subit' is impersonal, 'it comes up [into her mind]', and the whole memory follows in an accusative-and-infinitive ('hanc … detexisse'). The 'Lemnicola', the dweller on Lemnos, is Vulcan, whose fire-island it is; the motherless child is the one Minerva shut in a basket and gave to these three sisters with orders not to look. Aglauros looked. 'contra data foedera' is the language of a broken treaty, not of a broken promise between girls.

sentences.t:
et gratamque deo fore iam gratamque sorori
et ditem sumpto, quod avara poposcerat, auro.
sentences.l: and that now she would be dear to the god, and dear to her sister too, and rich with the gold taken up, which in her greed she had demanded.
sentences.i: and that now she would be welcome to the god, and welcome to her sister too, and rich with the gold she had greedily demanded.
sentences.n: The thought runs on in the same accusative-and-infinitive from 'Subit': what galls the goddess is not only the old crime but the reward coming to it. 'gratus' takes a dative and means welcome or pleasing to someone — not grateful, and not owed thanks: she would be welcome to the god and welcome to her sister, twice over. 'sumpto … auro' is an ablative absolute wrapped around its own relative clause. 'avara', 'greedy', is Minerva's word for her, not the poem's — and it is the word that will fetch Envy.

sentences.t:
Protinus Invidiae nigro squalentia tabo
tecta petit.
sentences.l: At once she makes for Envy's house, crusted foul with black rot.
sentences.i: At once she makes for the house of Envy, filthy with black decay.
sentences.n: 'tabum' is the discharge of a corpse or a wound; 'squalentia' is the caked filth of mourning and neglect. Invidia is a personified abstraction about to be given a house and a body, and Ovid will stop the story for thirty lines to build both. The Latin word is 'in-videre', to look upon — everything in the portrait will be about eyes.

sentences.t:
Domus est imis in vallibus huius
abdita, sole carens, non ulli pervia vento,
sentences.l: Her house is hidden away in the deepest of valleys, wanting sun, passable to no wind at all,
sentences.i: Her house lies hidden at the bottom of a valley, without sun, open to no wind,
sentences.n: 'carere' takes an ablative of the thing lacked, so 'sole carens' is 'wanting sun'. The description is built out of negatives — no sun, no wind, and in the next two lines no fire — which is how Ovid builds all his allegorical houses: by subtraction, until only the owner is left.

sentences.t:
tristis et ignavi plenissima frigoris, et quae
igne vacet semper, caligine semper abundet.
sentences.l: gloomy and utterly full of a sluggish cold, and such as is always empty of fire, always overflowing with murk.
sentences.i: gloomy, brim-full of a cold that will not move, a house always without fire and always thick with fog.
sentences.n: 'ignavi frigoris' gives the cold the adjective for a coward or a sluggard: cold that does nothing, in a house whose owner does nothing but look. 'vacet' and 'abundet' are subjunctives of characteristic — they describe the kind of house it is rather than report a fact about it. Empty and overfull are set in the same shape, one clause each.

sentences.t: Huc ubi pervenit belli metuenda virago,
sentences.l: When the maiden to be feared in war arrived here,
sentences.i: When the warrior maiden, the terror of battle, arrived,
sentences.n: 'metuenda' is a gerundive used as an adjective, 'to be feared', with 'belli' a genitive of respect: to be feared in the matter of war. 'virago' is a woman who does a man's work. Ovid sets the most active word in the language against the house of the thing that will not get up off the floor.

sentences.t:
constitit ante domum (neque enim succedere tectis
fas habet) et postes extrema cuspide pulsat.
sentences.l: she stopped in front of the house (for she has no right to go in under that roof), and strikes the doorposts with the very tip of her spear.
sentences.i: she stopped in front of the house — she is not permitted to pass under that roof — and struck the doorposts with the tip of her spear.
sentences.n: 'fas' is what divine law allows, as against 'ius', what human law allows: a goddess of the clear mind may not physically enter this house. So she knocks with a weapon, at arm's length, using the far end of it — 'extrema cuspide' — the way one touches a thing one does not want on one's hands.

sentences.t:
Concussae patuere fores. Videt intus edentem
vipereas carnes, vitiorum alimenta suorum,
Invidiam, visaque oculos avertit.
sentences.l: Struck, the doors stood open. She sees within, eating viper-flesh, the nourishment of her own vices, Envy; and, once she was seen, she turned her eyes away.
sentences.i: The doors shook and swung open. Inside she sees Envy eating snake-meat, the food that feeds her vices; and having seen her, she turned her eyes away.
sentences.n: 'patuere' is the poetic third-person plural perfect, short for 'patuerunt'. Read '-ere' as '-erunt' wherever the sense wants a plural past — Ovid uses this form constantly. The object of 'videt' is held back a line and a half, so that we are shown the meal before we are shown who is eating it; and Minerva, whose own weapon is a face on a shield, cannot look at this one.

sentences.l: But she gets up from the ground sluggishly, and leaves the bodies of the half-eaten snakes, and comes forward with a lifeless step;
sentences.i: But she gets up off the floor slowly, leaves the half-eaten snakes' bodies where they lie, and comes on at a listless walk;
sentences.n: 'humo' is a bare ablative, 'from the ground' — Envy has no chair. 'inerti' is the negative of 'ars': without skill, without force, unable to act. The four words 'passu incedit inerti' do what they describe, and the whole entrance is a delay.

sentences.t:
utque deam vidit formaque armisque decoram,
ingemuit vultumque ima ad suspiria duxit.
sentences.l: and when she saw the goddess, splendid in beauty and in arms, she groaned, and drew her face down into sighs from the depths.
sentences.i: and when she saw the goddess, splendid in her beauty and her armour, she groaned, and drew her face down into a sigh fetched from the bottom of her.
sentences.n: 'forma … armis' is an ablative of respect: splendid in respect of beauty and of arms. The point of the visit is that Envy is made to look at something excellent, which is the one thing she cannot bear. Magnus prints 'ima ad suspiria', the face drawn down towards sighs fetched from the depths; some editions print 'una ac', which makes her draw her face and her sighs together in one movement.

sentences.t:
Pallor in ore sedet, macies in corpore toto,
nusquam recta acies, livent rubigine dentes,
pectora felle virent, lingua est suffusa veneno.
sentences.l: Pallor sits in her face, wasting in the whole body; nowhere a straight glance; her teeth are livid with rust; her breast is green with gall, her tongue is flooded over with poison.
sentences.i: Pallor sits in her face, wasting in every limb; her look never goes straight; her teeth are livid with decay; her chest is green with bile, her tongue steeped in venom.
sentences.n: Six clauses with almost no connectives, two of them with no verb at all — 'macies in corpore toto', 'nusquam recta acies' — so that one 'sedet', 'sits', has to carry them. Latin can pile a portrait up like a list. 'nusquam recta acies': her eyes never go straight at anything, which is what the word 'invidia' is made of. Yellow-green bile was the body's seat of bitterness; pallor, rust, green — every colour here is the colour of something going bad.

sentences.t: Risus abest, nisi quem visi movere dolores.
sentences.l: Laughter is absent, except such as pains, once seen, have set going.
sentences.i: She never laughs, except at pain she has watched.
sentences.n: 'movere' is '-erunt' again, the plural perfect: 'have stirred'. 'quem' is a relative with its antecedent inside the main clause — 'except such laughter as'. The condition is exact and horrible: not laughter at pain reported, but at pain 'visi', seen, since seeing is the only pleasure she is capable of.

sentences.t: Nec fruitur somno, vigilacibus excita curis,
sentences.l: Nor does she have enjoyment of sleep, startled awake by wakeful cares,
sentences.i: Nor does she get any good of sleep, kept up by cares that will not sleep either,
sentences.n: 'fruitur' takes an ablative of the thing enjoyed, so 'somno' is 'in sleep' rather than 'sleep'. 'vigilacibus' is a rare adjective, cares that are themselves awake — the sleeplessness belongs to the cares, not to her, so it is not a punishment laid on from outside but simply what having this character is like.

sentences.t:
sed videt ingratos intabescitque videndo
successus hominum, carpitque et carpitur una,
suppliciumque suum est.
sentences.l: but she sees the successes of men, unwelcome to her, and by the seeing wastes away; and she gnaws and is gnawed at once, and is her own punishment.
sentences.i: but she sees men succeed, which she cannot bear, and wastes away with the seeing; she gnaws and is gnawed at the same time, and is her own punishment.
sentences.n: 'videndo' is an ablative gerund, 'by the act of seeing'. 'carpit … carpitur' sets one verb active and passive side by side with 'una', 'at one and the same time', holding them together: three words that do what the whole portrait argues. 'supplicium' is the word for a judicial penalty — she is not sentenced to anything, she is the sentence.

sentences.t:
Quamvis tamen oderat illam,
talibus adfata est breviter Tritonia dictis:
sentences.l: Yet although she hated her, the Tritonian addressed her briefly with words of this kind:
sentences.i: Hating her though she did, the Tritonian spoke to her — briefly:
sentences.n: 'Tritonia' is a cult-title of Minerva, from the Triton water by which she was said to have been born. 'breviter' is placed to be felt: the goddess will not stay in this house a syllable longer than the errand needs, and the speech that follows is twelve words long.

sentences.t:
“Infice tabe tua natarum Cecropis unam.
Sic opus est. Aglauros ea est.”
sentences.l: “Infect one of Cecrops' daughters with your rot. So there is need. She is Aglauros.”
sentences.i: “Infect one of the daughters of Cecrops with your rot. That is what is needed. Aglauros is the one.”
sentences.n: 'tabe' is the same word used of the filth caked on Envy's house: the goddess names her instrument by its discharge. 'opus est' is an impersonal idiom, 'there is need [of it]', the plainest way in Latin of saying that a thing must be so without saying who decided it. The order comes first, the reason is withheld, and the name is kept for last.

sentences.t:
Haud plura locuta
fugit et impressa tellurem reppulit hasta.
sentences.l: Having said no more, she fled, and with her spear pressed down thrust the earth away.
sentences.i: She said no more, but fled, pushing the ground away from her with a thrust of her spear.
sentences.n: 'impressa hasta' is an ablative absolute doing an instrument's work — the spear planted, and she vaults. 'reppulit tellurem' reverses the point of view: not she leaving the earth but the earth shoved off, which is how a leap feels from the inside. She uses the same spear she knocked with, and touches the place with nothing else.

sentences.t:
Illa deam obliquo fugientem lumine cernens
murmura parva dedit, successurumque Minervae
indoluit,
sentences.l: She, marking the goddess as she fled with a sidelong eye, gave out small mutterings, and was pained that it would go well for Minerva,
sentences.i: Watching the goddess go, with a look off to one side, she muttered a little, and it hurt her that Minerva's business would prosper,
sentences.n: 'obliquo lumine' — the sidelong look is Envy's only way of seeing, and the portrait has been building to it since 'nusquam recta acies'. 'successurum' is a future infinitive used impersonally, 'that it was going to turn out well for Minerva': what stings is not the errand but its success, in advance. 'indoluit' is grief specifically at another's good.

sentences.t:
baculumque capit, quod spinea totum
vincula cingebant, adopertaque nubibus atris,
sentences.l: and she takes up her staff, which thorn-bindings girdled the whole of, and, covered over with black clouds,
sentences.i: and takes up her staff, wrapped along its whole length in bands of thorn, and, hidden in black cloud,
sentences.n: 'totum' agrees with 'quod', the staff: the thorns go round the whole of it. Cloud is the standard cover for a god who does not wish to be seen travelling, and she takes it for what she is about to do. This is the third divine implement in a hundred lines — after Minerva's spear and Mercury's wand — and the only one that hurts to hold.

sentences.t:
quacumque ingreditur, florentia proterit arva
exuritque herbas et summa cacumina carpit,
sentences.l: wherever she walks she tramples the flowering fields and scorches the grasses and nips off the topmost shoots,
sentences.i: wherever she sets foot she tramples the fields in flower, scorches the grass, and nips the tops off the growing shoots,
sentences.n: 'carpit' is the same verb used of her gnawing at herself eleven lines back; here it is the gardener's word for pinching out a growing tip, which stops a plant without killing it — which is exactly what envy does in this poem. 'quacumque' is an indefinite relative adverb, 'by whatever way'.

sentences.t:
adflatuque suo populos urbesque domosque
polluit.
sentences.l: and with her breathing upon them she pollutes peoples and cities and houses.
sentences.i: and with a breath upon them she defiles whole peoples, cities, houses.
sentences.n: 'adflatus' is a breathing-upon, the word used of infection and of divine inspiration alike: the same act, and only the outcome tells them apart. The three nouns narrow as they go — people, city, house — and the last of them is where she is going. 'polluit' is a religious word: what she leaves behind is unfit for ritual use.

sentences.t:
Et tandem Tritonida conspicit arcem
ingeniis opibusque et festa pace virentem,
sentences.l: And at last she catches sight of the Tritonian citadel, green with talents and wealth and festal peace,
sentences.i: And at last she comes in sight of Minerva's citadel, in full green with genius and wealth and holiday peace,
sentences.n: 'virentem', growing green, answers 'virent' eighteen lines back, where Envy's chest was green with gall; now Athens is green with prosperity. Same colour, opposite meanings, eighteen lines apart. 'ingeniis' means the minds of the people — the city is rich in wits, the one wealth Envy cannot counterfeit.

sentences.t: vixque tenet lacrimas, quia nil lacrimabile cernit.
sentences.l: and she scarcely holds back her tears, because she sees nothing to weep at.
sentences.i: and she can hardly keep from weeping, because there is nothing in sight to weep at.
sentences.n: The best joke in the passage, and it is made entirely out of grammar: 'lacrimas' and 'lacrimabile' from the same root, one clause apart, with the cause inverted — she cries because there is no reason to cry. 'nil' is the contracted 'nihil', ordinary in verse.

sentences.t: Sed postquam thalamos intravit Cecrope natae,
sentences.l: But after she entered the bedchamber of the girl born of Cecrops,
sentences.i: But once she had entered the room of the daughter of Cecrops,
sentences.n: 'Cecrope natae' is 'of her born from Cecrops', an ablative of origin with a participle — Latin's neat way of saying 'daughter of'. Cecrops was the first king of Athens, and 'Cecropis' is Ovid's standing word for anything Athenian. The whole journey of cloud and blighted fields ends, quietly, in one girl's bedroom.

sentences.t:
iussa facit pectusque manu ferrugine tincta
tangit et hamatis praecordia sentibus implet,
sentences.l: she does what she was ordered, and touches her breast with a hand dyed the colour of iron-rust, and fills her insides with hooked briars,
sentences.i: she does as she was told: she touches the girl's breast with a hand stained iron-dark, and packs her innards with hooked thorns,
sentences.n: 'ferrugo' is the dark blue-red of rusting iron, the colour Latin gives to gloom and to the underworld. 'praecordia' are the parts under the heart, where a Roman kept his feelings, so filling them with thorn is not a metaphor but an operation. Note that she works with her hand: she could barely walk, and the one thing she does briskly is this.

sentences.t:
inspiratque nocens virus, piceumque per ossa
dissipat et medio spargit pulmone venenum.
sentences.l: and breathes into her a hurtful poison, and scatters the pitch-black venom through her bones and sprinkles it in the middle of her lung.
sentences.i: and breathes a hurtful poison into her, spreading the pitch-black venom through her bones and sprinkling it deep in her lungs.
sentences.n: 'inspirat' is literally 'breathes in' — the 'adflatus' that fouled whole cities, now delivered to one person. 'virus' in Latin is any foul liquid, slime or sap or poison, and carries nothing of our modern sense. Every verb here is a verb of distribution: nothing is broken, everything is filled.

sentences.t: Neve mali causae spatium per latius errent,
sentences.l: And so that the causes of the harm should not stray over too wide a space,
sentences.i: And so that the sources of the misery should not have to range too widely,
sentences.n: 'Neve' introduces a negative purpose clause, 'and so that … not'. 'latius' is a comparative used absolutely, 'rather too wide'. The reasoning is Envy's own and it is horribly practical: a poison works faster if the reasons for feeling it are kept close at hand. So she brings the pictures into the room.

sentences.t:
germanam ante oculos fortunatumque sororis
coniugium pulchraque deum sub imagine ponit,
cunctaque magna facit.
sentences.l: she sets before her eyes her sister, and the sister's fortunate marriage, and the god under a beautiful image, and makes everything large.
sentences.i: she sets her sister before her eyes, and her sister's lucky match, and the god in the handsomest shape she can give him — and makes it all bigger than it is.
sentences.n: 'ponere ante oculos' is the technical phrase from rhetoric for making an audience see what is not there; Envy is doing a trained orator's work on an audience of one. 'sub pulchra imagine' means the god is shown at his best, which is the cruelty of it. 'cuncta magna facit' is three words and the whole mechanism of envy: not lying — enlarging.

sentences.t:
Quibus inritata dolore
Cecropis occulto mordetur et anxia nocte,
anxia luce gemit,
sentences.l: Provoked by these things, the daughter of Cecrops is bitten by a hidden pain, and, in distress by night, in distress by day, she groans,
sentences.i: Goaded by all this, the daughter of Cecrops is gnawed by a pain she keeps hidden, and groans, wretched by night and wretched by day,
sentences.n: 'Quibus' is another connecting relative, in the ablative — 'and by these things'. 'mordetur' is the passive of the verb for biting, and it answers Envy's own 'carpitque et carpitur': the disease has been transferred intact. 'occulto' is the word that separates the two of them — Envy's misery is public and squalid, Aglauros's is hidden inside a rich house.

sentences.t:
lentaque miserrima tabe
liquitur ut glacies incerto saucia sole.
sentences.l: and most wretched she melts away with a slow rot, as ice does, wounded by an uncertain sun.
sentences.i: and, wretched past saying, melts in a slow wasting, like ice under a wounding, unreliable sun.
sentences.n: 'tabes' for the third time: the word that described Envy's house and Envy's poison now describes the girl. 'saucia' is a soldier's word — the ice is 'wounded' by the sun, which makes the gentlest imaginable cause into an injury. 'incerto sole' is the sun of early spring that comes and goes, so that the melting is never steady and never allowed to stop.

sentences.t: Felicisque bonis non lenius uritur Herses,
sentences.l: And by the good things of fortunate Herse she is burned no more gently
sentences.i: And her lucky sister Herse's good fortune burns her no more gently
sentences.n: The girl is melting ice in one line and burning scrub in the next: Ovid runs two opposite images at her within two lines, and both are of something consumed slowly and without a flame. 'Herses' is a Greek genitive ending, taken over whole from Greek as Latin poets do with Greek names. 'bonis' is 'by the good things', the plural noun for someone's blessings.

sentences.t:
quam cum spinosis ignis supponitur herbis,
quae neque dant flammas lenique tepore cremantur.
sentences.l: than when a fire is set under thorny weeds, which give no flames and are burned away with a mild warmth.
sentences.i: than a fire set under thorny weeds burns them — weeds that never flare, but are consumed at a low, mild heat.
sentences.n: 'supponitur' is literally 'is placed underneath', as fire is laid beneath a pile of scrub to burn it off. The whole point of the simile is the absence of flame: there is nothing to see, and the thing goes all the same. Magnus prints 'lenique tepore', 'with a gentle warmth'; some editions print 'lentoque vapore', 'with a slow steam'.

sentences.t:
Saepe mori voluit, ne quicquam tale videret,
saepe velut crimen rigido narrare parenti;
sentences.l: Often she wanted to die, so as not to see any such thing; often to tell it, as though a crime, to her stern father;
sentences.i: Often she wanted to die rather than see any of it; often to report it, as if it were a crime, to her hard father;
sentences.n: The second 'saepe' borrows its verb from the first — 'voluit' has to be heard again — which is why English needs nothing more than 'often to tell it'. 'velut crimen' gives her away: her sister's happiness is not an offence, and she knows it, but she would like to lay it before authority as though it were. 'rigido' is her adjective for her father, not the poem's.

sentences.t:
denique in adverso venientem limine sedit
exclusura deum.
sentences.l: at last she sat down on the threshold facing him, meaning to shut the god out as he came.
sentences.i: in the end she sat down in the doorway, right in his path, to shut the god out when he came.
sentences.n: 'exclusura' is a future participle of purpose — 'about to shut out', carrying the intention as well as the futurity. There is a joke folded into the word: the lover shut out on the doorstep is a whole genre of Roman love poetry, and Ovid has the girl sit down in the doorway and become the door herself.

sentences.t:
Cui blandimenta precesque
verbaque iactanti mitissima “desine” dixit:
sentences.l: To him, as he threw out coaxings and prayers and the gentlest words, she said “stop”:
sentences.i: As he poured out coaxing and pleading and the softest words he had, she told him: “Stop.”
sentences.n: 'Cui … iactanti' is a connecting relative with a participle, a whole clause packed into two agreeing words: 'and to him, while he was throwing out …'. 'iactanti' is a faintly contemptuous verb for talk, the same word as tossing something about. Against his three nouns of persuasion she has one word, and it is an imperative.

sentences.t: “hinc ego me non sum nisi te motura repulso.”
sentences.l: “I shall not be moving myself from here unless you have been driven off.”
sentences.i: “I am not moving from this spot until you have been driven off.”
sentences.n: 'motura sum' is a future participle with 'sum', the periphrastic future — 'I am going to move' — and 'me' makes it transitive: she will move herself, or she will not. 'te repulso' is an ablative absolute, 'with you beaten back'. She has made her own removal conditional on his defeat, which is a boast; the poem is about to take her at her word on the not-moving.

sentences.t:
“Stemus” ait “pacto” velox Cyllenius “isto”:
caelestique fores virga patefecit.
sentences.l: “Let us stand,” says the swift Cyllenian, “by that bargain of yours,” and with his heavenly wand he threw the doors open.
sentences.i: “Let us stand by that bargain of yours,” says the quick Cyllenian — and opened the doors with his heavenly wand.
sentences.n: 'stare pacto' is the legal idiom for abiding by an agreement, to stand by a compact: he takes her boast as a contract and holds her to it. Ovid breaks the phrase into three pieces around the speech-tag, 'Stemus … pacto … isto'; and 'isto' is the demonstrative meaning 'that of yours', with a sneer available inside it.

sentences.t:
At illi
surgere conanti partes, quascumque sedendo
flectimus, ignava nequeunt gravitate moveri.
sentences.l: But for her, as she tries to rise, the parts which we bend in sitting cannot be moved, for a sluggish heaviness.
sentences.i: But when she tries to get up, the parts we bend in order to sit will not move: a sluggish weight has them.
sentences.n: 'illi … conanti' is a dative of the person concerned. Ovid will not name the hips and knees — 'the parts we bend in sitting' — and the 'we' pulls the reader's own body into the sentence, so that you find yourself testing the joint as you read. 'ignava' is the adjective given to the cold in Envy's house: the paralysis is made of what she was infected with.

sentences.t: Illa quidem pugnat recto se attollere trunco,
sentences.l: She does fight to lift herself with her trunk straight,
sentences.i: She fights, certainly, to haul herself upright from the waist,
sentences.n: 'pugnat' with an infinitive is a poetic stretch of the verb for fighting a battle: she 'fights to raise'. 'truncus' is a tree's trunk and a body's torso at once, and it is doing quiet work here — the word the language uses for the part of you that is most like wood.

sentences.t:
sed genuum iunctura riget, frigusque per inguen
labitur, et callent amisso sanguine venae.
sentences.l: but the joint of the knees stiffens, and cold slides through the groin, and her veins go hard, the blood lost out of them.
sentences.i: but the knee-joint locks, and cold slips through the groin, and the veins harden as the blood goes out of them.
sentences.n: The change is reported upward, joint by joint, in the order a reader can feel it. 'amisso sanguine' is another ablative absolute, 'with the blood lost'. Two readings sit in these two lines: Magnus prints 'per inguen', through the groin, where some editions read 'per ungues', through the nails, and he prints 'callent', they grow hard or callous, the word used of a workman's hands, where some print 'pallent', they grow pale — easier, and much less physical.

sentences.t:
Utque malum late solet inmedicabile cancer
serpere et inlaesas vitiatis addere partes,
sentences.l: And as the canker, an evil past medicine, is accustomed to creep out wide and to add the unharmed parts to the ruined,
sentences.i: And as a canker, an evil no medicine touches, creeps out wide and adds the sound parts to the ruined,
sentences.n: 'cancer' is the crab and the spreading ulcer at once — the medical writers used the word of a growth whose veins run out like a crab's legs. 'inmedicabile' is Magnus's spelling, kept as the edition prints it. 'addere' is an accountant's verb: the disease does not destroy the healthy parts, it adds them to its own column.

sentences.t:
sic letalis hiems paulatim in pectora venit
vitalesque vias et respiramina clausit.
sentences.l: so the deadly winter came little by little into her breast, and closed the ways of life and the breathing-passages.
sentences.i: so the deadly winter worked its way little by little into her chest and closed off the channels of life, the passages of breath.
sentences.n: 'hiems' is winter and a storm at once: the cold that began in Envy's fireless house arrives here as a season. 'letalis … vitales' sets death against life across the two lines. 'respiramina' is a made-sounding noun from 'respirare' — the places where breath goes — and Ovid is fond of these coinages in '-men'.

sentences.t:
Nec conata loqui est, nec, si conata fuisset,
vocis habebat iter:
sentences.l: She did not try to speak; nor, if she had tried, did she have a road for her voice:
sentences.i: She did not try to speak; and if she had tried, she had no road left for a voice:
sentences.n: A mixed condition: the 'if' clause is pluperfect subjunctive, unreal, while the main verb stays in the plain imperfect indicative, which makes the fact blunter than a full unreal condition would — there simply was no passage. 'iter vocis', a road for the voice, picks up 'vitales vias' from the line before: the closing has reached her throat.

sentences.t:
saxum iam colla tenebat,
oraque duruerant, signumque exsangue sedebat.
sentences.l: stone already held her neck, and her face had hardened, and a bloodless statue sat there.
sentences.i: stone already had her throat, her face had set hard, and a bloodless statue sat where she was.
sentences.n: 'sedebat' is the verb she has been carrying since she sat down in the doorway, and it is also the ordinary verb for a statue standing in its place — one word does the sitting and the being-a-monument. 'signum' is the plain Latin word for a statue; 'exsanguis', bloodless, is exactly the word for marble and for a corpse.

sentences.t: Nec lapis albus erat: sua mens infecerat illam.
sentences.l: And the stone was not white: her own mind had stained her.
sentences.i: And the stone was not white: her own mind had dyed it through.
sentences.n: 'infecerat' is the dyer's verb — and it is the same verb Minerva used when she gave the order, 'Infice tabe tua', stain her with your rot. The command given fifty lines ago is discharged in the last word of the tale, and the colour of the stone is explained by the colour of the mind: nothing was added from outside that was not already inside her.
